opus-5.5.text:
I think a big part of it is that R&D is the most visible and legible part of the innovation process. When you think of technological progress, you picture labs, scientists, patents, papers. Those are easy to point to and easy to measure, so people naturally assign them a lot of credit. But when you look at how productivity actually improves in the economy, a large share of it comes from things that don't look like formal R&D at all.

Take learning by doing. Firms get better at producing things simply by producing more of them. Workers figure out small improvements on the factory floor, managers reorganize processes, supply chains get optimized. Wright's law, the observation that costs fall predictably with cumulative production, captures a lot of this, and it holds across many industries where formal research spending is a small part of the story. Solar panels and batteries are good examples. Some of the cost decline came from lab breakthroughs, but a large amount came from scaling up manufacturing and accumulating experience.

There's also the issue of complementary inputs. An idea by itself is not worth much unless you have the capital, the workforce, and the infrastructure to deploy it. If you look at historical growth, a lot of it is driven by scaling up: more people, more capital, more energy, and more tacit know-how spread across a big economy. R&D gets credit for the final result even though it was one input among many, and often not the binding one.

And when economists try to measure it, the returns to R&D at the margin, especially at the aggregate level, tend to look less impressive than the naive story suggests. Research spending and the number of researchers have grown enormously over the past several decades, yet productivity growth in frontier economies hasn't accelerated. It has arguably slowed. If R&D were the dominant driver, you'd expect that massive increase in research effort to show up more clearly in growth.

This matters for AI in particular. A common view is that AI will transform the economy mainly by automating science, building AI researchers that produce breakthroughs. I think that's too narrow. If most growth comes from broad automation of labor across the economy, with the experimentation, deployment, and learning that come with it, then the big impact of AI will come from doing ordinary work at scale, not just from a handful of AI scientists in a lab. That changes how you should think about the timeline and the shape of an AI-driven growth acceleration.

r001.rationale: The response describes growth as driven in part by scaling up people, capital, energy, and know-how, but does not say that long-run growth requires scaling all factors of production together.

r002.rationale: It discusses productivity growth and other growth inputs, but does not state that total factor productivity growth accounts for only a fraction of long-run growth.

r003.rationale: It says R&D is one input among many and describes productivity gains from non-R&D activities, but does not state that explicit R&D accounts for only a fraction of total factor productivity growth.

r004.rationale: The response says R&D is not the binding input in many cases, but does not distinguish its being essential for long-run growth from its accounting for most of that growth.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the main reason is that when people look at economic growth, they see this very visible thing, which is technological progress, and they naturally attribute most of the growth to it. And there's a sense in which that's correct. If you look at long-run growth, most of it does come from better technology, broadly construed. But the mistake is in equating technology with what gets produced by the formal R&D sector, by the people who are explicitly paid to do research and development.

If you actually look at the numbers, R&D spending in the US is something like three percent of GDP, and the share of the labor force that works in R&D is also quite small. And when economists try to estimate the returns to that investment, the returns are high, but they're not nearly high enough to account for all of total factor productivity growth. So there's a big residual that has to be explained by something else.

And I think what explains it is that a lot of what drives productivity growth is much more diffuse. It's learning by doing in firms, it's process improvements that nobody writes a paper about, it's people figuring out better ways to organize a factory or a supply chain. It's the accumulation of experience in a workforce, better management, better institutions, scale effects from larger markets. None of that shows up in R&D statistics, but it's probably a larger contributor than the formal research sector.

The other thing is that R&D is complementary to a lot of other inputs. You can have a great idea come out of a lab, but turning that into something that actually raises productivity requires capital investment, requires people who know how to use it, requires an economy that can absorb it. So even when you trace a productivity gain back to some piece of research, the research by itself wasn't sufficient. A lot of the value is created downstream in the diffusion and adoption process.

I think this matters for how people think about AI, because the naive story is that if you automate R&D, you get explosive growth, since R&D is where growth comes from. And I'd say that's too simple. If you only automate the research part and the rest of the economy still has to go through the slow process of adoption and capital accumulation and learning, then you get a boost, but not nearly as dramatic a one as people imagine. The really big effects come when you automate the broader economy, not just the people with PhDs in labs.

r001.rationale: The response says research gains need capital, skilled people, and adoption, but does not state that long-run growth requires scaling all factors of production together.

r002.rationale: It does not say that total factor productivity growth accounts for only a fraction of long-run growth; it discusses R&D accounting for only part of TFP growth.

r003.rationale: It says estimated returns to R&D are not enough to account for all TFP growth, leaving a residual explained by other factors.

r004.rationale: The response distinguishes formal R&D from broader sources of productivity growth, but does not state that R&D is essential for long-run growth.

astra-6.text:
I think people often conflate two claims. One is that technological progress is very important for long-run growth. The other is that spending more on R&D will substantially increase the long-run growth rate. The first can be true without the second being true.

Suppose discoveries become harder to make as you advance. You can put more researchers into a field and get more progress, but some of that extra effort is offset by the fact that you’re working on harder problems. In that kind of world, permanently increasing the share of the economy devoted to research might give you a period of faster growth and leave you permanently richer, without permanently raising the growth rate.

That’s a distinction people tend to miss: a higher level of income versus a higher rate of growth. If you assume an R&D intervention raises growth forever, those benefits compound, and you can get enormous estimates of its value. But that conclusion depends on how the production of new ideas works.

There’s also a counterfactual question. If a particular research project hadn’t happened, would the discovery never have occurred, or would another team have made it a few years later? The technology can be enormously valuable while the contribution of accelerating its discovery is considerably smaller. So I wouldn’t say R&D is unimportant. I’d say you have to be careful about moving from the importance of technology to the marginal value of additional research.

r001.rationale: The response discusses research effort and growth, but does not state that long-run growth requires scaling all factors of production together.

r002.rationale: It does not say that total factor productivity growth accounts for only a fraction of long-run economic growth.

r003.rationale: It does not state that explicit R&D accounts for only a fraction of total factor productivity growth.

r004.rationale: It distinguishes the importance of technological progress from the effects of additional R&D, but does not state that R&D is essential for long-run growth while accounting for less than most of it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think people often conflate two different questions: what determines the level of productivity, and what determines its long-run growth rate? R&D can be very important for the first without having as much influence on the second as you might initially think.

Suppose we permanently doubled the fraction of the economy devoted to research. You’d expect more innovation and faster productivity growth for a while. But if ideas become harder to find as technology advances, that additional research effort eventually gets absorbed by the increasing difficulty of making progress. You end up with a richer economy, but not necessarily a permanently higher growth rate.

In that kind of model, sustained growth depends more on how quickly research effort itself grows, rather than simply how much research we do. So pointing to inventions and saying, “These came from R&D, therefore R&D spending determines long-run growth,” skips an important step. You need to ask what happens as the research frontier moves, and how much additional effort is required to keep advancing it.

That doesn’t mean research is unimportant or that we shouldn’t fund more of it. A permanent increase in the level of productivity can be enormously valuable. It’s just a different claim from saying that more R&D permanently raises the growth rate.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss total factor productivity or say that it accounts for only a fraction of long-run growth.

r003.rationale: It does not say that explicit R&D accounts for only a fraction of total factor productivity growth.

r004.rationale: It says R&D can raise productivity and distinguishes a productivity-level increase from permanently faster growth, but does not state that R&D is essential for long-run growth while accounting for less than most of it.
